title: Intraocular Gas vs. Air Tamponades in Vitreoretinal Surgery
summary: A comprehensive clinical reference comparing intraocular air, SF6, C2F6, and C3F8 gas tamponades. Details physical properties, expansion kinetics, surgical protocols, safety warnings, and evidence-based indications for retina specialists and trainees.

sections.title: Definition & Fundamental Physics
content: **Intraocular Gas Tamponade**: Clear, inert, insoluble gas inserted into the vitreous cavity to provide internal retinal tamponade and seal retinal breaks.
**Surface Tension**: Gases exhibit high surface tension against aqueous humor (~70 mN/m), preventing fluid entry through retinal breaks.
**Buoyancy (Flotation Force)**: Upward force exerted according to Archimedes' principle; maximally effective superiorly at the apex of the bubble.
**Arc of Contact**: Dependent on overall gas bubble volume; a 1.0 mL bubble covers approximately 60 degrees, while a 2.0 mL bubble covers ~90-100 degrees of the retina.

branches: Phase 1: Expansion Phase (Nitrogen influx exceeds gas efflux)
Phase 2: Equilibrium Phase (Partial pressures equalize with bloodstream)
Phase 3: Dissolution Phase (Exponential decay via capillary diffusion)

sections.title: Pneumatic Retinopexy Step-by-Step Protocol
content: Step 1: Administer topical/peribulbar anesthesia and check baseline IOP.
Step 2: Perform anterior chamber paracentesis to lower IOP and create space.
Step 3: Inject 0.5-0.6 mL of pure (100%) SF6 or 0.3-0.4 mL pure C3F8 via pars plana (3.5-4.0 mm from limbus) using 30G needle, bevel up.
Step 4: Immediately tilt head to prevent gas escape and check CRA perfusion.
Step 5: Apply 'steamroller maneuver' if macula-on with subretinal fluid to push fluid away from fovea.
Step 6: Posture patient so bubble abuts the retinal break for 5-7 days post-procedure.

sections.title: Fluid-Gas Exchange (FGX) Protocol in Vitrectomy
content: Step 1: Complete core and peripheral vitrectomy; identify all retinal breaks.
Step 2: Place air-fluid exchange cannula near optic disc or posterior break.
Step 3: Initiate automated air infusion (30-35 mmHg) while aspirating fluid.
Step 4: Perform endolaser or cryopexy around all identified breaks under air.
Step 5: Flush vitreous cavity with non-expansile gas mixture (e.g., 20% SF6 or 12% C3F8) for 20-30 seconds to replace air.
Step 6: Suture sclerotomies tightly to prevent gas leak and hypotony.

sections.title: Critical Surgical Red Flags & Safety Warnings
content: CONTRAINDICATION: Nitrous Oxide (N2O) anesthesia must be discontinued at least 20 minutes BEFORE intraocular gas injection to prevent severe expansion and sudden IOP spike.

STRICT WARNING: Air travel, high altitude exposure, or unpressurized mountain travel is ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED while any intraocular gas bubble remains (risk of severe ocular ischemia and blindness).
INTRAOPERATIVE DANGER: Pure gas injection into a non-paracentesed eye or incorrect non-expansile mixing ratio can cause Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO).
FISH-EGGING HAZARD: Multiple small gas bubbles created during injection can migrate into subretinal space; inject in a single smooth motion with head tilted.
ANTERIOR CHAMBER MIGRATION: In aphakic or pseudophakic eyes with compromised capsules, gas can shift anteriorly, causing corneal endothelial decompensation and pupillary block.

sections.title: Complications & Clinical Management Protocols
content: **Early IOP Elevation**: Secondary to gas expansion or pupillary block. Manage with topical aqueous suppressants (beta-blockers, alpha-2 agonists, CAIs), oral Acetazolamide, or AC tap if CRAO occurs.
**Gas Feathering (Cataractogenesis)**: Posterior subcapsular 'feather-like' opacities caused by direct gas contact with lens back. Usually reversible if contact is brief; require positioning change.
**Subretinal Gas Migration**: Occurs if gas injected behind retina or through large break. Requires manual displacement or re-vitrectomy.
**Proliferative Vitreoretinopathy (PVR)**: Extended gas tamponade provides scaffold for PVR if serum proteins accumulate superiorly.

sections.title: Landmark Clinical Evidence & Advances
content: **PIVOT Trial (2019)**: Demonstrated that Pneumatic Retinopexy (PR) with SF6/C3F8 achieved superior 12-month visual acuity and lower morbidity compared to Vitrectomy (PPV) for primary rhegmatogenous RD meeting inclusion criteria.

**Air vs. SF6 in Macular Hole Repair**: Studies demonstrate comparable closure rates for small-to-medium (<400 μm) macular holes using Air vs. SF6, significantly reducing posturing duration for patients.
**Heavy Gas Mixtures & Isovolumetric Formulations**: Precise micro-dosing systems reduce the incidence of inadvertent hyper-expansion and postoperative ocular hypertension.

sections.title: High-Yield Clinical Pearls for Board Exams
content: **Nitrous Oxide Solubility**: N2O is 34 times more soluble in blood than N2, leading to rapid diffusion into the gas bubble and massive IOP spikes within minutes.
**Non-Expansile Gas Mixing Rule**: 20% SF6, 16% C2F6, 12% C3F8. Memory tip: The numbers decrease as the fluorine atom count increases!
**CRAO Management Post-Gas**: If central retinal artery is non-perfused post-op, perform immediate anterior chamber paracentesis to release volume.
**Optic Pit Maculopathy**: C3F8/SF6 combined with macular laser or vitrectomy successfully displaces retinoschisis fluid away from the macula.
